entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?

Both permanents end up controlled by Analia. Lay Claim targets Corrupted Conscience (an Aura is itself a permanent, so it's a legal target for Lay Claim's 'enchant permanent'). When Lay Claim resolves, it becomes attached to Corrupted Conscience, and its text 'You control enchanted permanent' gives Analia control of Corrupted Conscience [110.2b], [701.3c].

Now Corrupted Conscience's own text says 'You control enchanted creature' (referring to Bane Alley Blackguard, the creature it's attached to). That 'you' is a reference to whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience -- the Aura's controller is a separate, independently-tracked thing from the enchanted creature's controller [303.4e]. Since Analia now controls Corrupted Conscience (via Lay Claim), the 'you' in Corrupted Conscience's control-granting text now means Analia, so Analia also gains control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

Note this is different from the Lay Claim ruling that says gaining control of a creature doesn't automatically give you control of Auras attached to it [Lay Claim ruling #0] -- that's the reverse direction (creature -> Aura). Here the flow is the other way: Analia took control of the Aura (Corrupted Conscience) directly via Lay Claim, and Corrupted Conscience's own ability is what then hands her the creature.

So after Lay Claim resolves: Corrupted Conscience is controlled by Analia (attached to Bane Alley Blackguard, per Lay Claim's effect), and Bane Alley Blackguard is also controlled by Analia (per Corrupted Conscience's 'you control enchanted creature' effect, since Analia is now that Aura's controller). Nico ends up controlling neither permanent. Lay Claim remains controlled by Analia, its caster, as normal [110.2b]. This analysis assumes a two-player game (Nico and Analia); the rules given don't address any multiplayer wrinkle here, and none appears needed since only two players are involved in this control chain.

entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. Iroas, God of Victory is a non-Aura enchantment other than Starfield of Nyx, so this applies to it.

Iroas, God of Victory's own printed ability ("As long as your devotion to red and white is less than seven, Iroas isn't a creature") is also a type-changing effect, and both effects modify the same characteristic (card type) in the same layer — layer 4, type-changing effects [613.1d]. Type-changing effects that apply in layer 4 are processed in order, and later-applying effects act on whatever the current type already is [613.6]. Because Starfield of Nyx's creature-granting effect only starts applying at the moment Alan controls five enchantments (i.e., the moment Starfield of Nyx itself resolves and joins the battlefield), it is the more recently applied layer-4 effect compared to Iroas, God of Victory's own long-standing "isn't a creature" clause. As a result, Starfield of Nyx's "is a creature in addition to its other types" effect is the one that determines Iroas, God of Victory's final type: it is a creature (in addition to being a Legendary Enchantment Creature — God, per 205.1b/205.2b/300.2, which let an object satisfy effects for any of its combined card types). This happens regardless of whether Alan's devotion to red and white ever reaches seven — the two abilities are independent, and Starfield of Nyx's grant simply wins the type determination here.

Once Iroas, God of Victory is established as a creature, Starfield of Nyx's power/toughness-setting clause (layer 7b) also applies to it, setting its base power and toughness each equal to its mana value. Iroas, God of Victory's mana cost is {2}{R}{W} (2 generic, {R}, {W}), giving a mana value of 4. So its base power and toughness become 4/4, overriding the printed 7/4 (though it keeps Indestructible, giving creatures you control menace, and preventing damage to attacking creatures you control, since those aren't affected by this layer).

Note: this conclusion holds no matter what Alan's actual devotion to red and white turns out to be — the given devotion-to-white value of 2 doesn't change the outcome, since Starfield of Nyx's effect isn't conditioned on devotion at all.

Note that rule [305.7] also says setting a land's subtype "doesn't add or remove any card types (such as creature) ... the land may have," so if Murmuring Bosk had already become a creature by some other means before Blood Moon applied, it would keep the creature card type while switching from Forest to Mountain. But since Life and Limb's own creature-granting clause is gated on the Forest/Saproling subtype and Murmuring Bosk no longer qualifies once Blood Moon applies, no such creature status is ever granted to it here.

entries.question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?

entries.question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?

Since the top card of Aiden's graveyard is Mistform Skyreaver, a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter's characteristic-defining ability gives it "the full text" of Mistform Skyreaver — meaning it takes on Mistform Skyreaver's name, mana cost, color, types, abilities (Flying and "{1}: This creature becomes the creature type of your choice until end of turn."), power, and toughness, per rule [612.6] and Volrath's Shapeshifter's own reminder text and [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Yixlid Jailer's static ability ("Cards in graveyards lose all abilities") strips abilities from cards sitting in graveyards, but it does not rewrite or erase the printed text of those cards. Volrath's Shapeshifter's full-text ability is a characteristic-defining ability, and per rule [604.3] such abilities key off of an object's printed characteristics and function in all zones; nothing in Yixlid Jailer's effect (or in the general rule about copiable values not incorporating other non-copy effects, [707.2a]) causes the loss of abilities to carry over into what Volrath's Shapeshifter reproduces. In short, Yixlid Jailer stops Mistform Skyreaver itself from having Flying while it's in the graveyard, but it doesn't stop Volrath's Shapeshifter from acquiring Flying by reading Mistform Skyreaver's printed text.

So Volrath's Shapeshifter becomes (in relevant part) a flying creature named Mistform Skyreaver with power/toughness 6/6, the mana-type-changing activated ability, and its own "{2}: Discard a card" ability layered on top.

This assumes there's no other effect in play altering the text itself (as opposed to just removing abilities) of Mistform Skyreaver; if some other effect had literally rewritten Mistform Skyreaver's text to remove Flying (rather than just stripping abilities the way Yixlid Jailer does), the outcome could differ.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Watchwolf] enchanted by [Lignify], [Figure of Destiny] that's had its third ability activated, and [Swab Goblin]. They casts [Pack's Favor] targeting Swab Goblin. After that resolves, they casts [Mirrorweave] targeting Figure of Destiny. What are the characteristics of Swab Goblin and Watchwolf?

entries.answer:
Right after Mirrorweave resolves: Swab Goblin becomes a copy of Figure of Destiny (name "Figure of Destiny", mana cost {R/W}, color red/white, card type Creature — Kithkin, base power/toughness 1/1, with all three of Figure of Destiny's printed activated abilities, none of which have been activated on this new copy), and it is currently 4/4 because the +3/+3 from Pack's Favor is still applying on top of that base. Mirrorweave's text is "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn" (Mirrorweave). Figure of Destiny is nonlegendary, so it's a legal target, and it is itself excluded from "each other creature." Both Swab Goblin and Watchwolf therefore become copies of Figure of Destiny.

What gets copied is only the copiable values of Figure of Destiny — the values derived from its printed text (name, mana cost, color, types, rules text, power/toughness) [707.2a][707.2]. Figure of Destiny had its third ability activated, meaning it is currently a Kithkin Spirit Warrior Avatar, 8/8, with flying and first strike (Figure of Destiny). But that transformation is the result of resolving one-shot effects from its own activated abilities, not a characteristic-defining ability or an "as...enters" effect, so it is not part of the copiable values — exactly like the Chimeric Staff example in rule 707.2, where a Clone copying an artifact that had turned itself into a 5/5 Construct via an activated ability copies only the original artifact, not the 5/5 creature (it does still get the ability that could turn it into a creature again). So both Watchwolf and Swab Goblin copy Figure of Destiny as a 1/1 Kithkin creature with mana cost {R/W} (making it red/white in color) and its three printed activated abilities, base power/toughness 1/1 — not the 8/8 flying first-strike Avatar form.

The +3/+3 until end of turn from Pack's Favor (Pack's Favor) is a separate, ongoing continuous effect on the permanent, unrelated to the copy operation — copy effects don't erase other continuous effects already affecting the object [707.4] — so it still applies on top, making Swab Goblin's current power/toughness 4/4 until end of turn.

Since the copy effect resolves in layer 1 [613.2a] and Lignify's type/ability/P-T effects apply in the later layers that govern type, abilities, and power/toughness, Lignify's effects are applied after — and override — the copied Kithkin type, the three copied abilities, and the copied 1/1 base power/toughness. Both Mirrorweave's copy effect and Pack's Favor's +3/+3 last only until end of turn; once the turn ends, Swab Goblin will revert entirely to being itself (2/2 Goblin Pirate), and Watchwolf will revert to being Watchwolf again — at which point Lignify will reapply to make it a 0/4 Treefolk with no abilities, the same end state it was in before Mirrorweave was cast.

entries.question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?

Duplicant becomes a 4/4 after its imprint ability resolves.

Here's why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has 3 +1/+1 counters on it while on the battlefield, giving it a base 1/1 plus +3/+3 = 4/4. When Duplicant's "Imprint" ability exiles Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, Skullbriar's own printed ability ("Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library") is active in the zone it's leaving (the battlefield), so its counters remain on it as it goes to exile. Per rule [122.1a], a +1/+1 counter modifies an object's power and toughness even in a zone other than the battlefield, and this is confirmed for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave specifically by [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] and [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5] (Skullbriar in a non-battlefield zone with a +1/+1 counter has its power/toughness increased accordingly, and it keeps all its counters, not just some). [Duplicant ruling #2] clarifies that characteristic-defining abilities (like a */* creature's defining ability) apply to the exiled card for this purpose, but abilities that merely add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's static ability) do not apply while the card sits in exile, since those effects are ordinarily battlefield-only continuous effects. Counters, however, are not abilities — rule [122.1a] makes clear a +1/+1 counter directly modifies the card's power and toughness in any zone, including exile — so this restriction does not exclude Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's counters. Duplicant therefore reads Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's power and toughness as 4/4 (including its counters) and takes on those values, becoming a 4/4 (overriding its printed 2/4), still a Shapeshifter with no other creature types since a Zombie Elemental's types would normally also be copied, but that detail isn't part of the power/toughness question asked.

This assumes there is no ability like Yixlid Jailer or similar in play removing abilities from cards in exile or graveyards; if such an effect were active, per [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1] Skullbriar's counter-retention ability could be shut off and the counters would not carry over, which would change the outcome.

entries.question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?

With Leyline of Singularity present, both Awoken Demon and the token end up legendary and share the same name (Awoken Demon, per rule 111.13's principle that a token copy takes the copied permanent's name), so the legend rule in rule 704.5j triggers: Ainsley must choose one of the two identically-named legendary permanents to keep, and the other goes to the graveyard [704.5j][Leyline of Singularity ruling #2]. This exception-vs-static-effect interaction is also consistent with how rule 707.9f says copy exceptions are evaluated based on the copy effect's own instructions, not effects from other permanents like Leyline of Singularity [707.9f]. This answer assumes a normal two-player or multiplayer game where only Ainsley controls both permanents; the legend rule works the same in multiplayer since rule 704.5j is not player-count dependent.

entries.question: Addison controls [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove] and casts [Blood Moon]. What are the characteristics of [Snow-Covered Island], [Study Hall], [Dryad Arbor], and [Mountain] after Blood Moon resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that printed-basic lands keep their basic supertype and gain all five basic land types from Dryad, while nonbasic lands (including Study Hall and Dryad Arbor) become Mountains due to Blood Moon in timestamp order, with Dryad Arbor remaining a creature land.
entries.answer:
Blood Moon splits Addison's lands into two groups: lands that are already basic (unaffected by Blood Moon) and lands that are nonbasic (which Blood Moon strips down to nothing but Mountain), while Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's static ability keeps trying to add all five basic land types to every land Addison controls.

Why the split happens: rule [205.4c] says a land is "basic" only if it has the supertype "basic" printed on it - having a basic land type (like Forest or Mountain) doesn't make a land basic if it lacks that supertype. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's ability only grants land types, not the "basic" supertype [Dryad of the Ilysian Grove ruling #0], so it never changes which of Addison's lands count as "nonbasic" for Blood Moon's purposes.

Because Dryad of the Ilysian Grove has been on the battlefield first and Blood Moon is cast afterward, Dryad's type-adding effect has the earlier timestamp and Blood Moon's type-setting effect has the later one; in layer 4 the later (Blood Moon) effect is applied on top of the earlier one. Rule [305.7] explains what a "setting" effect like Blood Moon's does: it strips away the land's old land types and any abilities generated from its rules text or old land types (though it doesn't strip abilities granted by unrelated effects, and per this same rule it never removes card types or supertypes). Blood Moon's own rulings confirm this: "Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" [Blood Moon ruling #2], and this doesn't touch names or supertypes [Blood Moon ruling #1].

Applying this to each land:

- **Snow-Covered Island**: This is a *basic* land ("Basic Snow Land — Island"), so Blood Moon's "nonbasic lands are Mountains" clause never applies to it [205.4c]. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's effect still adds all five basic land types "in addition to its other types" [305.7], so it becomes Basic Snow Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest, keeping the Basic and Snow supertypes [205.4b], with all five mana abilities: {T}: Add {W}, {T}: Add {U}, {T}: Add {B}, {T}: Add {R}, {T}: Add {G} [305.6].

- **Mountain**: Also a *basic* land ("Basic Land — Mountain"), so it too is untouched by Blood Moon's nonbasic clause. Dryad of the Ilysian Grove adds the other four basic types in addition, so it becomes Basic Land — Plains Island Swamp Mountain Forest with the same five mana abilities as above.

- **Study Hall**: This is a *nonbasic* land (no "basic" supertype). Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's earlier-timestamp effect first tries to add all five basic land types to it, but Blood Moon's later-timestamp setting effect then overwrites it: per [305.7] and [Blood Moon ruling #2], it loses all its land types (including the ones Dryad granted) and all abilities generated from its rules text - so its "{T}: Add {C}" and "{1}, {T}: Add one mana of any color..." abilities are gone - and it becomes a plain Land — Mountain with only "{T}: Add {R}."

- **Dryad Arbor**: This is a Land Creature — Forest Dryad with no "basic" supertype, so it too counts as nonbasic under [205.4c] even though Forest is itself a basic land type. The same sequence applies: Dryad of the Ilysian Grove's addition of all five basic types is wiped out by Blood Moon's later setting effect, which removes its old land type (Forest) and the intrinsic "{T}: Add {G}" ability that came with it [305.6, 305.7], replacing it with the land type Mountain and "{T}: Add {R}." Blood Moon does not touch card types or creature subtypes [305.7], so Dryad Arbor remains a Land Creature — Mountain Dryad, still a 1/1, still green from its color indicator, and still a creature (with the usual summoning-sickness/non-spell rules for lands played as creatures) [Dryad Arbor ruling #0, Dryad Arbor ruling #2, Dryad Arbor ruling #3].

One timing note: this assumes Dryad of the Ilysian Grove was already on the battlefield before Blood Moon resolved (as the question states), giving Dryad's effect the earlier timestamp. If the order were reversed (Blood Moon already active, then Dryad of the Ilysian Grove entering later), Dryad's addition would apply after Blood Moon's setting effect and the nonbasic lands would instead end up with all five basic types (Mountain plus the other four), since nothing would come along afterward to strip them away again.

entries.answer_gold:
Snow-Covered Island and Mountain have all basic land subtypes: "Plains", "Island", "Swamp", "Mountain", and "Forest". Dryad of the Ilysian Grove doesn't change supertypes and Blood Moon affects nonbasic lands.

Study Hall has subtype Mountain. There are no dependencies between Dryad of the Ilysian Grove and Blood Moon, so we apply the type-changing effects in timestamp order.

Dryad Arbor is now a Creature Land - Dryad Mountain. Gaining a basic land type doesn't remove other card types or nonland subtypes.

entries.question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
entries.reason: The candidate claims Alayna's Thespian's Stage becomes a full copy including its copy ability, but the reference says both Thespian's Stages end up only with the Alpine Moon–granted "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and no other abilities.
entries.answer:
Assuming a two-player game between Nico and Alayna (the rules given only address the two-player framing of "opponent"), here's the end state of each permanent:

1) Nico's Thespian's Stage (the one already copying Temple of Triumph): It becomes a bare, nameless-in-function land called "Temple of Triumph" with only one ability: "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Reason: when Thespian's Stage copied Temple of Triumph, its copiable values (including its name, its "enters tapped" ability, its scry-on-ETB ability, and its "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" ability) became Temple of Triumph's values, and its own activation clause was folded back in as "except it has this ability" (707.3, 707.9b). Once Alayna's Alpine Moon resolves naming "Temple of Triumph," its text ("Lands your opponents control with the chosen name lose all land types and abilities, and they gain '{T}: Add one mana of any color'") applies to Nico's Thespian's Stage because it is currently named Temple of Triumph and controlled by Alayna's opponent (Alpine Moon's own text overrides the general rules for that permanent). It loses every ability it has — including the folded-in "becomes a copy of target land" ability — and gains only the mana-of-any-color ability (Alpine Moon; Alpine Moon ruling #1 confirms only types/abilities are stripped, not supertypes or other card types, though Temple of Triumph has none of those to lose anyway). So this Thespian's Stage can no longer activate a copy ability at all while this effect persists.

2) The actual Temple of Triumph land being targeted: assuming Nico also controls this real Temple of Triumph (it's also named "Temple of Triumph" and is an opponent's land from Alayna's perspective), Alpine Moon strips it the same way — it loses its land types and all abilities (enters-tapped, the scry trigger, and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}") and gains "{T}: Add one mana of any color" (Alpine Moon). If instead Alayna herself controls that real Temple of Triumph, Alpine Moon would not touch it at all, since Alpine Moon only affects lands "your opponents control."

3) Alayna's second Thespian's Stage, after its activated ability resolves targeting that real Temple of Triumph: it becomes a full, functional copy of Temple of Triumph's ordinary printed characteristics — Land type, "This land enters tapped" (won't retrigger, since Thespian's Stage was already on the battlefield — Thespian's Stage ruling #1), "When this land enters, scry 1" (also won't trigger, same ruling), and "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" — plus it keeps "{2},{T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability." It is unaffected by Alpine Moon's stripping effect even though its name is now also "Temple of Triumph," because Alayna controls it and Alpine Moon only hits lands her opponents control. Crucially, the order of events doesn't matter here: even though Alpine Moon resolved first, Thespian's Stage's copy effect only looks at Temple of Triumph's copiable values — the printed values as modified only by other copy effects, never by non-copy effects like Alpine Moon's ability/type removal (Thespian's Stage ruling #3, "counters and other effects aren't copied"). So the second Thespian's Stage copies a clean, unstripped Temple of Triumph regardless of whether Alpine Moon already hit the real Temple of Triumph.

In short: Nico's Thespian's Stage and (if Nico controls it) the real Temple of Triumph both end up as bland lands with only "{T}: Add one mana of any color" and no other abilities, while Alayna's second Thespian's Stage becomes a full, working copy of Temple of Triumph (including its own copy ability), untouched by Alpine Moon because Alayna controls it.

entries.answer_gold: Both Thespian's Stages are lands named "Temple of Triumph" and have "{T}: Add one mana of any color." and no other abilities. Because Thespian's Stage gains its ability as part of the copying process, the ability applies in the copy layer, which is earlier than the adding and removing abilities layer.

entries.question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Kenrith's Transformation remains attached (and therefore keeps stripping abilities and setting P/T), whereas the correct ruling is Kenrith becomes attached to an illegal object and is put into the graveyard, after which Thraben Purebloods regains its prior characteristics except that it is only an enchantment.
entries.answer:
Once One with the Stars resolves, Thraben Purebloods stops being a creature altogether and becomes just a green, ability-less Enchantment permanent (with no creature subtype), while still being enchanted by both Kenrith's Transformation and One with the Stars.

Here's why, working through the continuous-effects layers (rule 613.7, 613.9):

- Layer 4 (card type): Kenrith's Transformation has an earlier timestamp and turns Thraben Purebloods into a green Elk creature, losing its other types (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3). One with the Stars has a later timestamp and says "Enchanted permanent is an enchantment and loses all other card types." Because timestamp order decides which type-setting effect "wins" when neither depends on the other (613.9), One with the Stars' effect is the one currently determining Thraben Purebloods' types: it is now only an enchantment, no longer a creature at all. Since the creature type is gone, the Elk creature subtype goes with it (One with the Stars ruling #2 - subtypes tied to a lost card type are removed).

- Layer 5 (color): Nothing overrides Kenrith's Transformation's color-setting, so Thraben Purebloods stays green.

- Layer 6 (abilities): Kenrith's Transformation's "loses all abilities" effect already started applying to Thraben Purebloods before the type change happened. Rule 613.6 says that once an effect starts applying to an object in a given layer, it keeps applying to that object in that layer even if something later changes the object's other characteristics. So Thraben Purebloods still has no abilities. One with the Stars' "It still has its abilities" is just reminder text describing the general rule for permanents that stop being creatures - it doesn't grant an ability, so it doesn't restore anything Kenrith's Transformation stripped away (see 604.3 on how set characteristics/abilities interact, and 613.6 on effects continuing across layers).

- Layer 7b (power/toughness): Kenrith's Transformation's "base power and toughness 3/3" also keeps applying per 613.6, even though Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature; that P/T value is simply irrelevant while it isn't a creature.

So the practical result: Thraben Purebloods sits on the battlefield as a green, ability-less enchantment, enchanted by two Auras (Kenrith's Transformation and One with the Stars), with a dormant "3/3" characteristic that would matter again only if something later made it a creature.

One caveat: Kenrith's Transformation's own enchant restriction is "Enchant creature," and Thraben Purebloods is no longer a creature. Magic has a state-based action that puts an Aura into its owner's graveyard if it's attached to an object that no longer matches its enchant restriction, but that specific state-based-action rule was not provided in the rules given to me, so I can't confirm from the supplied material whether Kenrith's Transformation would fall off as a result. If you need that resolved, the relevant rule is the one governing Auras attached to illegal permanents.

entries.answer_gold:
Thraben Purebloods becomes an enchantment with no abilities and with the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an illegal target and is put into the graveyard. Thraben Purebloods then regains all characteristics except its type is only enchantment. State-based actions are checked again. Nothing happens, and Allen gets priority.

This is an interaction of continuous effects, so the layers will need to be considered. In this case, no changes occur until layer four. There are two effects occurring in this layer, so timestamps will need to be considered. Since Kenrith's Transformation was attached first, Thraben Purebloods maintains its status as a creature. Then, One with the Stars turns Thraben Purebloods into an enchantment and removes all other types. Thraben Purebloods is changed to the color dictated by Kenrith's Transformation in layer five. Thraben Purebloods loses all abilities in layer six due to Kenrith's Transformation. Lastly, Thraben Purebloods has its power and toughness set to the values stated in Kenrith's Transformation in layer seven. When state-based actions are checked, Kenrith's Transformation is attached to an enchantment and is put into the graveyard. State-based actions are checked again, and nothing happens.

entries.question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
entries.reason: The candidate wrongly claims the merged permanent gains and triggers Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability, while the reference correctly states the object is a face-down 2/2 with no abilities so Gnarr's ability does not trigger.
entries.answer:
The result is a single merged permanent, face down, that is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name and no creature types, but it has the mutate-triggered ability from Trumpeting Gnarr (and it can still be turned face up for the mana cost of whatever card Soul Summons manifested, if that card is a creature card).

Here's why: Soul Summons puts the top card of Avery's library onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature (manifest). Trumpeting Gnarr is then cast for its mutate cost {3}{G/U}{G/U} targeting that manifested creature. As the mutating creature spell resolves, it doesn't enter the battlefield as a new permanent; instead it merges with the target creature, becoming one object represented by both cards ([702.140c], [608.3d], [730.2e], [730.1]). Avery, as the mutating spell's controller, chooses whether Trumpeting Gnarr goes on top or on the bottom; here Avery chooses to leave the manifested card on top (i.e., Trumpeting Gnarr goes underneath).

For a mutated permanent, its non-ability characteristics (name, types, mana cost, power/toughness, etc.) come only from the topmost card or token, while it gains the abilities of every component card/token ([702.140e]). Since the topmost component here is the manifested card and it is still face down, its copiable characteristics are the standard face-down baseline: a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no types, and no mana cost, exactly as described for face-down objects ([707.3]). Trumpeting Gnarr's own printed name, types, and 3/3 stats are on the bottom and don't show through, but its ability "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" still applies to the merged permanent, per the rule that a mutated permanent has all abilities of each component ([702.140e], Trumpeting Gnarr). That ability triggers on this very mutate event, so Avery also gets a 3/3 green Beast creature token as a side effect, separate from the merged permanent itself.

Because the ability to turn a manifested card face up for its mana cost (if it's a creature card) belongs to the manifested card as manifested, that ability also carries over as one of the merged permanent's abilities ([702.140e]; Soul Summons). So the merged permanent can still be turned face up later for that card's own mana cost if it is a creature card; if it is turned face up, its characteristics would then become the printed characteristics of that card layered with Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities, per how merged/copy characteristics interact in layer 1a ([613.2a]).

This reasoning does not depend on the number of players at the table; nothing about targeting or turn order among multiple opponents changes how mutate or manifest resolve here, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

entries.answer_gold: It is a 2/2 colorless face-down creature with no abilities. It is face-down because the topmost object is face-down, and this status defines its characteristics. This notably means that Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability won't trigger.

entries.question: April casts [Spontaneous Flight] targeting their [Mist Dragon]. After that resolves April then activates its 'lose flying' ability. They cast another Spontaneous Flight targeting Mist Dragon. After that resolves they then use [Hex Parasite] to remove one flying counter. Does Mist Dragon have flying?
entries.reason: Both conclude Mist Dragon has flying because the second flying counter's grant has a later timestamp than the activation that caused it to lose flying, so the remaining counter still grants flying.
entries.answer:
Yes — after all these actions, Mist Dragon still has flying.

Here's the sequence of continuous effects and their timestamps:

1. April casts Spontaneous Flight (copy #1) targeting Mist Dragon. It resolves, giving +2/+2 until end of turn and putting a flying counter on Mist Dragon. This flying counter creates a continuous effect granting flying, with a timestamp at the moment it was placed (call it t1).
2. April then activates Mist Dragon's own "{0}: This creature loses flying" ability. This ability's effect ("loses flying," lasting indefinitely) resolves and gets a timestamp later than t1 (call it t2). Since this "loses flying" effect and the flying-counter's "has flying" effect don't depend on each other, they're compared purely by timestamp order, per [613.9] and [613.7a]: the later effect (t2, lose flying) wins, so at this moment Mist Dragon does **not** have flying.
3. April casts Spontaneous Flight (copy #2) targeting Mist Dragon again. It resolves, giving another +2/+2 and putting a second flying counter on Mist Dragon. This second counter's flying-granting effect gets a timestamp later than t2 (call it t3). Now the most recent gain-flying effect (t3) outranks the loses-flying effect (t2), so Mist Dragon **has flying again**. This mirrors [113.10c]'s principle that when two or more effects add and remove the same ability, the most recently created one prevails, and [702.9c] confirms that having flying from two counters at once is simply redundant, not a stronger or different state.
4. Hex Parasite then removes one flying counter from Mist Dragon (X=1, using {1}{B/P} or paying life for the Phyrexian mana). Mist Dragon now has one flying counter left instead of two. Hex Parasite's ability removes a *counter*, not an ability directly — it isn't the kind of "loses flying" effect covered by [113.10b] (which would strip out every instance of an ability at once). Since one flying counter remains, the flying-granting continuous effect tied to that remaining counter is still active, and — because it stems from the more recent Spontaneous Flight (t3), which is later than the timestamp of the "loses flying" activation (t2) — flying is still in effect for Mist Dragon.

Assumption: I'm treating each flying counter's flying-grant as getting its own timestamp equal to when that counter was placed, following the general timestamp principle in [613.7a]/[613.9]. The provided rules don't include a dedicated rule spelling out timestamps for keyword counters specifically, so if the game instead treated the "has flying because of a counter" condition as a single effect whose timestamp never advances past its very first appearance (t1), the remaining counter's effect would be older than the loses-flying activation (t2), and Mist Dragon would not have flying. Under the more standard reading used above (each new counter's grant counts as a fresh, later-timestamped effect), Mist Dragon has flying at the end of this sequence.

This is a single-player action sequence with no opponents or targeting/blocking involved, so nothing here differs between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Keyword counters and ability-removing effects all apply in layer 6 in timestamp order. However when April put the second flying counter on Mist Dragon all flying counters on Mist Dragon had their timestamps updated to match the most recent counter. Meaning that the remaining flying counter on Mist Dragon has a newer timestamp than the activation of the ability that causes it to lose flying.

entries.question: Aimee controls [Fiend Artisan] and has four creature cards in their graveyard. Nico enchants it with [Mystic Subdual]. What is the power and toughness of Fiend Artisan?
entries.reason: Both answers reach the same conclusion — Mystic Subdual removes Fiend Artisan's +1/+1-per-graveyard- creature ability (layer 6) and then applies -2/-0 (layer 7), leaving its printed 1/1 changed to -1/1.
entries.answer:
Fiend Artisan ends up as a -1/1 creature. Mystic Subdual gives Fiend Artisan "loses all abilities," which strips away Fiend Artisan's own static ability ("This creature gets +1/+1 for each creature card in your graveyard"). That ability-granting effect is applied in layer 6, before power/toughness-modifying effects in layer 7 are applied (rule 613.1's layer ordering), so once Fiend Artisan has lost all its abilities it no longer has the ability that was generating the +1/+1-per-graveyard-creature-card bonus (a layer 7c modifying effect per rule 613.4c). With that self-bonus gone, Fiend Artisan falls back to its printed base power and toughness of 1/1 (rule 302.4c: start with the printed numbers, then apply remaining continuous effects). Mystic Subdual's own -2/-0 effect is not one of Fiend Artisan's own abilities -- it comes from the Aura itself -- so "loses all abilities" doesn't remove it, and it still applies as a layer 7c modifying effect (613.4c) on top of the base 1/1. That gives 1-2 power and 1-0 toughness, i.e. -1/1. This mirrors the logic in Mystic Subdual's own ruling: when an enchanted creature's power/toughness depended on an ability it possessed, losing all abilities removes that effect first, leaving only the printed/base values for Mystic Subdual's -2/-0 to modify (with a */* creature that becomes 0/0, then -2/0). Fiend Artisan isn't a */* creature with a characteristic-defining ability -- its 1/1 is printed, and its pump is a separate static ability -- but the same principle applies: once that ability is gone, only the base printed 1/1 remains for Mystic Subdual to reduce. So the graveyard count (four creature cards) becomes irrelevant while Mystic Subdual is attached, since the ability that would count them no longer exists on Fiend Artisan.

entries.answer_gold: Fiend Artisan is a -1/1. In layer 6 Mystic Subdual eliminates the abilities of Fiend Artisan. In layer 7 Mystic Subdual gives Fiend Artisan -2/-0, making it a -1/1. Its ability to gain +1/+1 from each creature card in Aimee's graveyard does not apply, as it was removed.

entries.question: Nico controls [Humility]. Avalyn controls [Maritime Guard] and wants to cast [Glowstone Recluse] mutating onto the Maritime Guard and putting it on top. What will the resulting creature's P/T be?
entries.reason: Both conclude the merged creature ends up as a 1/1 with no abilities and won't get the mutate-triggered +1/+1 counters because Humility continuously sets base P/T and removes abilities.
entries.answer:
The mutated permanent will be a 1/1, and it will not get any +1/+1 counters from its mutate trigger. Here's why:

When Glowstone Recluse's mutate spell resolves targeting Maritime Guard, Maritime Guard doesn't die and a new creature doesn't enter the battlefield. Instead Glowstone Recluse merges with Maritime Guard to become one object represented by two cards, per rule [702.140c] and [608.3d]. Because Avalyn chose to put Glowstone Recluse on top, the resulting mutated permanent's other characteristics (including printed power/toughness) come from Glowstone Recluse (2/3), while it gains all abilities of both component cards — Reach and 'Whenever this creature mutates, put two +1/+1 counters on it' from Glowstone Recluse, and whatever Maritime Guard has (nothing, since it's a vanilla 1/3) — per rule [702.140e].

However, Nico's Humility is a continuous effect that says 'All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1.' This applies to every creature on the battlefield, regardless of who controls it. Base power/toughness for a creature normally starts at its printed value and then continuous effects are applied ([302.4c]); Humility's power/toughness-setting effect applies in layer 7b, the layer for effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific value ([613.4b]), and it overrides the 2/3 that would otherwise come from the merge. So the mutated Glowstone-Recluse/Maritime-Guard permanent ends up as a 1/1.

Humility also strips all abilities from that creature. Because Humility applies continuously (not as a one-time, timestamped snapshot), the mutated permanent never actually has its 'whenever this creature mutates' ability or Reach while Humility is affecting it — those abilities are suppressed the instant the merged permanent exists. As a result, the mutate-trigger ability that would put two +1/+1 counters on the creature does not exist to trigger, so no counters are added (this mirrors how Humility's ability-stripping and other characteristic-setting effects interact continuously and simultaneously, as shown in the Humility/Opalescence layering example in [Humility ruling #2]).

So the end result: a 1/1 creature with no abilities (no Reach, no counters), represented by both the Glowstone Recluse and Maritime Guard cards as one mutated permanent.

entries.answer_gold: 1/1 with no abilities, since mutate impacts the creature in layer 1 and Humility acts in layers 6 and 7. It will also not trigger Glowstone Recluse because Humility applies constantly and it's never on the battlefield without being affected.

entries.question: Alex controls [Magus of the Moon] and [Forgotten Monument]. Neil casts [Lizard, Connors's Curse] targeting Magus of the Moon. After Lizard, Connors's Curse has resolved, what are the characteristics of Forgotten Monument?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling: Forgotten Monument remains a nonbasic Mountain named "Forgotten Monument" that only taps for {R}, because Magus of the Moon's subtype-changing effect is applied in layer 4 before the layer-6 loss-of-abilities from Lizard, Connors's Curse.
entries.answer:
Forgotten Monument ends up being a nonbasic land named "Forgotten Monument" with the land type Mountain (in place of Cave) and only the ability "{T}: Add {R}" — it loses its printed "{T}: Add {C}" ability and its ability that grants other Caves a mana ability, and it does not become named "Mountain," gain the basic supertype, or gain any color.

Here's why: Alex's Magus of the Moon has the static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." Forgotten Monument (Land — Cave, with no basic land type) is a nonbasic land, so per [Magus of the Moon ruling #4], it "loses any other land types and abilities they had. They gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability '{T}: Add {R}.'" This matches the general rule [305.7]: setting a land's subtype to a basic land type strips its old land type and rules-text abilities and gives it the appropriate basic-land mana ability. Per [Magus of the Moon ruling #1], this effect doesn't touch names or supertypes, so Forgotten Monument keeps its name and does not gain the basic supertype (it's still a nonbasic land, just with the Mountain land type).

The key wrinkle in your scenario is that Neil's Lizard, Connors's Curse resolves and its Lizard Formula ability targets Magus of the Moon, causing Magus of the Moon to lose all abilities and become a 4/4 green Lizard creature. You might expect this to shut off the Mountain-making effect and let Forgotten Monument revert to being a Cave. entries.question: Ari controls [Magus of the Moon] enchanted with [Ichthyomorphosis]. Is Ari's [Dormant Volcano] a Mountain?

Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" is a type/subtype-changing effect, which is applied in layer 4 of the continuous-effects system [613.1d]. Ichthyomorphosis's effect that says the enchanted creature (Magus of the Moon) "loses all abilities" is an ability-removal effect, which is applied in layer 6. Rule [613.6] establishes that when an effect applies across multiple layers, each part is applied in its own layer regardless of when the generating ability was created or removed — and the official Magus of the Moon ruling confirms this exact scenario directly: "If Magus of the Moon loses its abilities, it continues to turn nonbasic lands into Mountains. This is because effects that change subtypes are applied before considering effects that remove abilities, regardless of the order in which those effects started" [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

So Dormant Volcano — being a nonbasic land — is turned into a Mountain: it loses its other land types and its printed abilities (its "enters tapped" ability, its sacrifice trigger, and its "{T}: Add {C}{R}" mana ability), and instead gains the land type Mountain along with the mana ability "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4]. Note that this doesn't make it a *basic* Mountain — Magus of the Moon's effect doesn't grant the basic supertype, so it remains a nonbasic land with the Mountain type, and it isn't renamed "Mountain" [Magus of the Moon ruling #1]. It also isn't a creature (Ichthyomorphosis's Fish-creature effect is on Magus of the Moon, a different permanent, not on Dormant Volcano), so that has no bearing here.

One clarification: the fact that Magus of the Moon itself has "lost all abilities" from Ichthyomorphosis does not stop this land-type-setting effect from continuing to apply, per the ruling cited above — this is a case where the two effects interact across different layers rather than one simply overriding the other.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Continuous effects are applied in a specific order, and type-changing effects are applied before ability-removing effects.

entries.question: Averie controls [Muraganda Petroglyphs] and [Wayward Angel], and has more than 7 cards in their graveyard. Nathan casts and resolves [Humility]. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics?

entries.answer:
Wayward Angel ends up as a black 6/6 Creature — Angel Horror with no abilities at all. Here's how the layers work out, given Averie has 7+ cards in the graveyard (so Wayward Angel's threshold ability is active) and both Muraganda Petroglyphs and a resolved Humility are on the battlefield:

Wayward Angel's threshold ability ("As long as there are seven or more cards in your graveyard, this creature gets +3/+3, is black, has trample, and has ...") is a normal static ability, not a characteristic-defining ability, because it only sets a characteristic (color) conditionally, which fails the CDA test in [604.3a]. So its effects (color change, +3/+3 boost, granted trample/upkeep-sacrifice ability) are applied in the normal layer system [613.1], each in its own layer: color in layer 5, granted abilities in layer 6, and the +3/+3 boost in layer 7c.

Humility's text "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1" also splits across layers: losing abilities is a layer 6 effect, and setting base power/toughness to 1/1 is a layer 7b effect [208.4b] (base P/T is the value after CDAs and P/T-setting effects, before +/- modifiers).

Applying the layers in order:
- Layer 5 (color): Wayward Angel's threshold ability is still fully intact at this point (layer 6 hasn't stripped anything yet), so per the Wayward Angel ruling it becomes black only, not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #0].
- Layer 6 (abilities): Humility removes all of Wayward Angel's abilities — flying, vigilance, trample, the sacrifice-a-creature trigger, and the threshold ability itself. As the Humility rulings show for the analogous Humility/Opalescence case, an ability that's already been used to produce effects in an earlier layer (like layer 5's color change) or that still has effects scheduled for a later layer keeps producing those effects even after the ability itself is stripped in layer 6 — "the rest of it will apply even if the permanent loses its ability before it's finished applying" [Humility ruling #2][Humility ruling #0]. So Wayward Angel's +3/+3 from threshold still lands later, even though the ability granting it is now gone.
- Layer 7b (base P/T): Humility sets Wayward Angel's base power and toughness to 1/1.
- Layer 7c (P/T modifiers): Two effects apply here — Wayward Angel's own threshold effect still contributes +3/+3 (per the reasoning above), and because Wayward Angel now genuinely has no abilities (they were all stripped in layer 6), Muraganda Petroglyphs' "Creatures with no abilities get +2/+2" also applies, adding +2/+2 [113.2a] (this is a quality/boost, not a granted ability, so it doesn't reintroduce any "ability" that would disqualify it).

Final math: base 1/1 (Humility) + 3/+3 (threshold, still lingering) + 2/+2 (Muraganda Petroglyphs) = 6/6.

So Wayward Angel is: black, Creature — Angel Horror, no abilities, base power/toughness 1/1, actual power/toughness 6/6. Its mana cost {4}{W}{W} is unchanged since neither effect touches mana cost.

Note on timing: this assumes Wayward Angel and Muraganda Petroglyphs were already on the battlefield before Humility was cast (as the question implies), giving Wayward Angel's threshold ability an earlier timestamp than Humility. If instead Humility had somehow existed before Wayward Angel's ability, the layer-6 removal order would differ, but since Humility's only layer-6 effect is a blanket "lose all abilities," the end result (no abilities) would be the same either way.

- In layer 5, Wayward Angel becomes black. 
- In layer 6 there are two contending effects: Wayward Angel's ability giving it trample and an upkeep triggered ability, and Humility's ability removing all abilities from Wayward Angel. There is no dependency between the two, since Wayward Angel's ability has already started applying in a previous layer, and will continue to apply even if removed by Humility's ability. entries.question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?

entries.question: Ari casts [Aeve, Progenitor Ooze], with two spells having been cast before then. Nadia controls [Humility]. What will Ari's battlefield look like once the stack fully resolves and state-based actions are checked?

This "enters with counters" effect is a replacement effect that modifies the event of entering the battlefield itself (614.1 describes replacement effects as "shields" around the event they modify), and rule 616.1g shows the same pattern: a self-referential "as this enters" ability is applied as part of each object's own entry, not preempted by other ongoing continuous effects. This removes the now-already-used "enters with a counter" ability and the "isn't legendary if it's a token" ability from all three Aeve permanents, and sets each one's base power and toughness to 1/1. Because Humility's text specifically sets "base" power and toughness (not power and toughness outright), and a +1/+1 counter is itself a +1/+1 modifier rather than a base-setting effect, the counters already placed in step 3 should still add on top of that 1/1 base — but the exact layer rule that orders counter application relative to base-setting effects isn't among the rules I was given, so I can't cite a rule confirming the final numbers (e.g., whether the original Aeve ends up 3/3). Normally that would trigger the rule requiring a player to keep only one legendary permanent of a given name, but that rule (commonly called the "legend rule") was not included in the rules given to me, so I can't tell you here whether/how Ari would have to clean that up.

entries.question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?

Here's why: at the moment Natalie casts One with the Stars, Allen's crew activation is still on the stack and hasn't resolved, so Capenna Express is only an artifact — it is not yet a creature, and it isn't an enchantment either. One with the Stars can only target 'creature or enchantment' (its printed Enchant restriction), so Capenna Express does not meet the legal-target requirements for that Aura at the time it is cast, and it still doesn't meet them when One with the Stars would try to resolve (since Capenna Express's crew ability, being lower on the stack, hasn't resolved yet either).

Since Capenna Express's own crew ability doesn't reference One with the Stars at all, it resolves normally and Capenna Express becomes a 6/6 artifact creature until end of turn, with no lingering enchantment effect from One with the Stars (which never attached).

Note the contrast with the One with the Stars ruling: it's only when the Aura actually resolves and attaches while the Vehicle is already a creature (or as it becomes a creature) that the 'stays an enchantment forever' effect kicks in [One with the Stars ruling #1]. Here, because One with the Stars was on top of the stack and had to check its target before Capenna Express ever became a creature, that attachment never happens.

This assumes the timing as given: Natalie's casting of One with the Stars happens strictly before the crew ability resolves, so One with the Stars sits above the crew activation on the stack and resolves first.
